idiom_name: fixture functions requested by parameter name
implementation_notes: The dedicated mother class is rare in Python: pytest fixtures in conftest.py are the dominant realization - a fixture function returns a fully valid domain object, is composable (fixtures request other fixtures) and is function-scoped by default, so every test gets a fresh instance. Plain module-level factory functions such as vip_customer(**overrides) serve unittest-style suites and shared helper packages, and factory_boy moves the same idea to declarative factories. Write the classic factory class only when construction is genuinely stateful (allocating unique identities across a run).
pitfalls: Session- or module-scoped fixtures hand the same object to many tests; a test that mutates it changes the fixture for every later test (the classic shared-fixture aliasing bug).
Fixture arguments are injected by parameter name: an autouse fixture hides dependencies, and a misspelled parameter only surfaces at collection time as a fixture-not-found error.
Mutable default arguments in factory functions (def customer(tags=[])) are shared across calls; use None and build the container inside.
Fixtures that open a database or network connection silently turn unit tests into integration tests and couple cleanup and ordering to the runner.

variants.name: Declarative factories with factory_boy
variants.idiom_name: factory.Factory subclass with Meta.model and lazy attributes
variants.implementation_notes: factory_boy is the fixtures-replacement library for Python: a Factory subclass declares the model in Meta plus attribute defaults, and build()/create()/stub() choose whether the object is unsaved, persisted or a plain attribute bag; LazyAttribute, Faker and SubFactory compose dependent objects. Adopt it once tests need per-case variation, ORM session handling or randomized realistic values, and keep a few pytest fixtures as named aliases for the canonical scenarios.
variants.code_sketch:
class CustomerFactory(factory.Factory):
    class Meta:
        model = Customer

    id = 7
    name = "Ada Lovelace"
    tier = Tier.VIP

customer = CustomerFactory.build(name="Grace Hopper")
pitfalls: create() must follow DjangoModelFactory/SQLAlchemyModelFactory to persist; with the plain Factory it silently returns an unsaved object and tests can pass for the wrong reason.
Faker-driven attributes are random: reseed via factory.random.reseed_random(...) or assertions on generated values flake.
Factory inheritance chains (SubFactory/RelatedFactory) can cascade into far more database writes than the test intended.
